title: Maritime NDT & Class Audit Support | Portsmouth, Virginia
description: NAVSEA, class and owner audit prep for Portsmouth, VA contractors: written practice, Examiner, procedures and records by an ASNT Level III. Contact us.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting & Class Audit Support in Portsmouth, Virginia
html:
If your company performs NDT inside Norfolk Naval Shipyard, gauges ships in Hampton Roads for class surveys, or supplies inspection services to the offshore wind work staged in Portsmouth, an audit of your NDT program is part of the job. Atlantis NDT is an ASNT NDT Level III consulting practice that gets contractors ready for those audits: written practice, procedures, examinations, personnel and equipment records, a rehearsal audit, and help answering findings. Share your contract clause or audit letter and we will map out the preparation.

Portsmouth's waterfront: a public naval shipyard and a wind port

Norfolk Naval Shipyard carries the name of the city across the river, but it stands in Portsmouth, on the west bank of the Southern Branch of the Elizabeth River. NAVSEA's own history fact sheet describes a yard that has operated continuously for more than 250 years: the Navy chose the old Gosport Shipyard in 1798 and bought the site from Virginia in 1801. Its Dry Dock 1, built between 1827 and 1833, is still on the property and is the yard's National Historic Landmark. Today the operational base covers about 1,275 acres including annexes in Portsmouth and Chesapeake, with five operable dry docks, and its work is repairing, overhauling and modernizing ships, aircraft carriers and submarines.

The number that matters to an NDT contractor is a different one. Alongside its civilian workforce and military personnel, the shipyard reports that between 1,500 and 3,000 contractor employees work there on a given day. Many of them weld, fit, insulate, paint or inspect, and the ones who inspect bring their company's NDT program through the gate with them. That program is judged against the Navy's requirements, not the habits a firm built up on commercial work.

Downriver, the Portsmouth Marine Terminal has taken on a second identity. Skanska began redeveloping 72 acres and 1,500 feet of wharf there in 2022, and the Virginia Port Authority announced the finished offshore wind staging hub in March 2025. Turbines and monopiles for Dominion Energy's 176-turbine, 2.6-gigawatt wind farm off Virginia Beach are gathered and loaded out from that site. Inspection work around it answers to the developer and the project's verification parties rather than to the Navy or a class society.

Working inside Norfolk Naval Shipyard as a contractor

At a government shipyard, the cognizant Government inspector for NDT is the shipyard itself, under its commander, rather than a Supervisor of Shipbuilding as at a private yard. Contractors performing NDT on Navy ships and systems there work to NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, Revision 1, dated 11 September 2014, which sets the minimum requirements for qualifying NDT personnel, procedures and equipment. The contract, the work package or the applicable NAVSEA standard items tell you which publications apply to a given job, and the drawing or specification supplies the acceptance criteria.

Navy work follows NAVSEA requirements, not class rules. A firm that has spent years gauging tankers to UR Z17 or testing hull welds for an ABS surveyor will find that much of its paperwork transfers poorly. The publication defines an "activity" as the sites of an organization under the same quality assurance management and plan, and the activity is the unit that holds the written practice, appoints the Examiner, qualifies procedures and certifies people. Two divisions of the same company operating under separate quality plans can therefore need separate arrangements. Our pages on NAVSEA NDT requirements for shipyards and the T9074 written practice go through the definitions clause by clause.

What NAVSEA's NDT publication changes for a commercial NDT firm

TopicTypical commercial practice under SNT-TC-1AUnder T9074-AS-GIB-010/271What it means for your files
Status of SNT-TC-1AGuidance the employer adapts in its written practiceInvoked, as modified, as mandatory minimumsEvery hour, examination and record your written practice promises must be met, not interpreted
RecertificationUp to five years, sometimes on evidence of continued performanceBy examination, at least every three years for operators and inspectors and every five for ExaminersExamination records must exist for each cycle; performance-based renewal will not pass
Ongoing oversightDefined by the employer, often informallyDocumented annual surveillance of each operator and inspector, plus technical performance evaluationsDated surveillance records become an audit item
Near-vision testJaeger J2 or equivalent, annuallyJaeger J1 at 12 to 16 inches, annuallyOld vision forms that record J2 are not enough
Prior certificationsThe employer decides whether to accept themNot transferable between activities except as NAVSEA authorizesA new hire from another yard is recertified by your activity
ProceduresApproved by the Level IIIApproved by the cognizant Examiner and qualified by demonstrating detection of known discontinuitiesA purchased or borrowed procedure is not usable until your activity qualifies it

The table is a summary. The publication itself, and any contract-specific modifications, decide. We read both with your quality manager before drafting anything.

What the government side samples during an audit

Government reviews of a contractor's NDT tend to start with the written practice and then go straight to people. Expect a reviewer to pick a handful of technicians who worked on recent jobs and ask for each one's training record, experience record, the general, specific and practical examinations with grades, the most recent vision test, and the certification signed by the activity. They will check the dates against the work: a technician whose certification or vision test had lapsed on the day of an inspection is a finding even if the weld was sound.

The second focus is procedures. The reviewer looks for the Examiner's approval, the qualification record that shows the procedure found the discontinuities it was meant to find, and evidence that the version on the job was the approved one. Equipment comes third: calibration certificates, reference standards and the checks recorded before and after use. The last is the annual oversight trail, which many firms new to Navy work simply do not have. If you need to build one quickly, our T9074 audit preparation page lists the evidence, and our experience log and vision record services rebuild the personnel side.

Whether an outside Level III can hold your activity's Examiner role is governed by the publication and the government inspector's acceptance. Where an outside Examiner is used, the activity still has to prepare and administer that Examiner's specific examination independently of the person being tested. We explain those mechanics plainly at the start, so nobody discovers them during the audit.

Boundaries: reactor plant work, radiography and welding

Much of the shipyard's workload involves nuclear-powered carriers and submarines. Work on naval nuclear propulsion plants follows its own requirements and is outside Atlantis's scope; we do not consult on it. Underwater NDT on Navy ships is also handled under a separate NAVSEA procedure rather than T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, and we flag that when a contractor's scope includes diving work.

Radiography is common on Navy repair work, but it is a method Atlantis does not perform on US soil. Where your company or its subcontractor holds the radioactive materials license and performs RT, our Level III can review the RT procedure and the radiographs. Welding procedure and welder qualification belong to the welding side of your organization; we do not write or qualify welding procedures and stay on the NDT side.

Commercial ships in Hampton Roads and class approval for gauging

Not all of Portsmouth's maritime NDT is Navy work. Commercial ships calling at Hampton Roads terminals, and those repaired at private yards across the river, still need thickness measurements for class surveys. Those measurements fall under IACS UR Z17, which requires the gauging company to hold approval from each ship's class society and to renew thickness measurement approval at intervals of no more than three years. The society reviews the company's documents, audits its office and watches a practical demonstration before it issues a certificate naming the services covered.

A firm that does both Navy and commercial work needs a written practice broad enough to satisfy both, or two clearly separated programs. The Navy's stricter recertification and vision rules can be applied company-wide, which keeps one set of personnel files compliant for both customers. Our IACS service supplier approval guide covers the class side, and the Norfolk maritime consulting page describes the private repair market on the other bank.

Offshore wind staging at Portsmouth Marine Terminal

Components that pass through a staging port are inspected on arrival, during storage and before load-out, mostly for transport damage, coating condition and secondary steel. The NDT rules for that work come from the developer's specifications and the project's quality plan, with third-party verification arranged by the project, not from class rules or NAVSEA. Inspection firms supporting that work are typically audited by the developer or its installation contractor, who want to see a written practice, method procedures, certification under the scheme the specification names, and calibrated equipment. Our US offshore wind NDT consulting page explains the wider program.

Because staging work is short and intense, the usual audit failure is a crew mobilized from another job with paperwork written for that job. If you expect to bid this work, align your procedures with the developer's specification before mobilization rather than after the first audit.

How an engagement runs for a Portsmouth contractor

Atlantis has no office in Virginia; we work from Houston, handle document work remotely, and come to Portsmouth for the parts that need to happen in person. Our Level III work is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, whose ASNT NDT Level III certificates cover five methods (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT) and who brings more than 11 years of international field experience. A Navy-side engagement normally moves through these steps:

  1. Clause review: we list the NDT obligations created by your contract, its referenced publications and the work packages you expect.
  2. Program comparison: we compare your written practice, procedures and records against those obligations and show the gaps in a single register.
  3. Rewrite: we draft the written practice and procedures to meet the publication, for approval by your management and your Examiner.
  4. Examinations and records: we help prepare written and practical examinations and rebuild personnel files, including oversight and vision records.
  5. Procedure qualification: we plan and witness qualification demonstrations on representative specimens with known discontinuities.
  6. Rehearsal and response: we audit your program the way the government reviewer will and help close any findings with evidence.

Your activity certifies its people and owns its records, the government inspector accepts or rejects them, and the class society, where one is involved, decides on approval. If you need a procedure written or qualified from scratch, see procedure development and procedure qualification and demonstration.

Atlantis and class approval: current status

For the commercial side of this page, one fact should be clear. Atlantis is at present seeking IACS UR Z17 approval from DNV, ABS and Lloyd's Register for its own thickness measurement work, and it has not yet received a class certificate from any of them. We prepare other firms for these audits while going through them ourselves, and we do not present Atlantis readings as class-credited until a society certifies us.

What to send us

  • The contract NDT clauses, referenced NAVSEA publications or standard items, or the class society's checklist.
  • Your written practice, and the name and qualifications of your current Examiner or Level III.
  • The NDT procedures you use on Navy or class work, with any qualification records.
  • Three personnel files, including examination grades, vision tests and oversight records.
  • Your equipment and calibration list and two recent inspection reports.
  • Previous audit findings and your responses.

We reply within one business day. For technician training, see maritime NDT training for Norfolk and Hampton Roads and our maritime NDT training overview.

Portsmouth readiness checklist

  1. Confirm which work is under NAVSEA publications, which is under class rules and which is under a developer's specification.
  2. Check that your written practice treats SNT-TC-1A as mandatory minimums for Navy work and states three-year recertification by examination.
  3. Pull every technician's vision record and confirm it shows Jaeger J1 at the required distance within the last year.
  4. Confirm each procedure used on Navy work carries Examiner approval and a qualification record from your activity.
  5. Verify that new hires from other yards were recertified by your activity, not accepted on prior certificates.
  6. Assemble the annual oversight records for every operator and inspector.
  7. If you gauge commercial ships, list your class approvals and their expiry dates.
  8. Review your radiography subcontractor's license, procedure and personnel files if RT is in scope.

For the national overview see maritime NDT audit support; neighboring Hampton Roads coverage is on our Newport News maritime page, and broader Level III work in the city is on the Portsmouth consulting page.

faq.q: Do contractors at Norfolk Naval Shipyard follow class rules for NDT?
faq.a: No. Navy work follows NAVSEA requirements, chiefly T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 for personnel, procedures and equipment, with acceptance criteria from the drawing or contract. Class rules apply to commercial ships, not to Navy work at the shipyard.

faq.q: Who audits a contractor's NDT program at a public naval shipyard?
faq.a: At a government yard, the cognizant Government inspector is the shipyard under its commander. At a private yard doing Navy work, that role belongs to the Supervisor of Shipbuilding. Prime contractors can also audit their subcontractors.

faq.q: Can our technicians keep the certifications they earned at another shipyard?
faq.a: Not automatically. T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 prohibits transferring NDT certifications between activities except as NAVSEA authorizes, so your activity recertifies new hires under its own written practice.

faq.q: Why did our vision records fail a Navy review?
faq.a: The usual reason is the near-vision standard. SNT-TC-1A refers to Jaeger J2 or equivalent, while the NAVSEA publication calls for Jaeger J1 at 12 to 16 inches, tested annually. See our vision examination records service.

faq.q: Does Atlantis consult on naval nuclear propulsion work?
faq.a: No. Reactor plant work is outside our scope. We support NDT programs for non-nuclear Navy and commercial work.

faq.q: Can Atlantis carry out radiography for us at the shipyard?
faq.a: No; Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. If you or a licensed subcontractor perform RT, our Level III can review the procedure and the radiographs.

faq.q: Is a procedure we bought from a consultant ready to use on Navy work?
faq.a: Not until your activity's Examiner approves it and it has been qualified by demonstrating detection of known discontinuities. Procedures are not transferable between activities without NAVSEA approval. We help plan and witness the qualification.

faq.q: Will someone from Atlantis come to Portsmouth or Norfolk?
faq.a: Yes, when the work needs it. Atlantis keeps no office in Virginia; reviews and drafting happen remotely from Houston, and we travel to Hampton Roads for mock audits, procedure qualifications and floor observations.

faq.q: Is Atlantis approved by a class society for thickness measurement?
faq.a: Not yet. Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, ABS and Lloyd's Register so that its own gauging work can be class-credited; no society has issued it a certificate so far.

faq.q: What NDT rules apply to inspection at the offshore wind staging terminal?
faq.a: The developer's specification and the project's quality plan, with third-party verification arranged by the project. Neither NAVSEA rules nor class rules govern that staging work by default. See offshore wind NDT consulting.
